transmission-line-001.question: A 50 Ω resistor terminates a lossless line with a characteristic impedance Z0 = 50 Ω. Which statement is correct?
choices: Total reflection occurs at the termination, and a standing wave forms on the line
No reflection occurs, and the voltage amplitude is the same everywhere on the line (VSWR = 1)
The reflection disappears only when the line length is an odd multiple of λ/4
transmission-line-001.explanation: When the load equals the characteristic impedance, the reflection coefficient is Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0) = 0, and all the power of the incident wave is absorbed by the load. With no reflected wave there is no standing wave, the voltage amplitude is the same everywhere on the line, and VSWR = 1. Total reflection occurs when the line is terminated in a short, an open or a pure reactance. With a matched termination, the input impedance also stays 50 Ω regardless of the line length. A length of λ/4 matters only for impedance transformation when the load is not matched.

transmission-line-002.question: Which correctly describes the characteristic impedance Z0 of a transmission line?
choices: The voltage-to-current ratio of a wave traveling one way on the line; it is set by the L and C per unit length and does not depend on the length
The DC resistance of the line's conductors summed over the whole length, so it is 0 for a lossless line
It grows as the line gets longer, in proportion to the total inductance of the whole line
transmission-line-002.explanation: The characteristic impedance is the ratio of voltage to current for a traveling wave with no reflection. On a lossless line it is set by the inductance L and capacitance C per unit length as Z0 = √(L/C). For example, with L = 250 nH/m and C = 100 pF/m, √2500 = 50 Ω. It depends only on the cross-sectional shape and the materials, and does not change however many meters of line you use. The DC resistance of the conductors causes loss, but it is not Z0 itself. What changes with length is the input impedance when a mismatched load is connected.

transmission-line-003.question: A 50 Ω line is terminated in a 100 Ω resistor. What is the voltage reflection coefficient Γ at the load?
transmission-line-003.explanation: Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0) = (100 − 50)/(100 + 50) = 50/150 = 1/3 ≈ 0.33. When the load is larger than Z0, Γ is positive and the reflected voltage at the load is in the same direction (in phase) as the incident wave. −1/3 comes from reversing the numerator to Z0 − ZL; it is the value for a termination of 25 Ω, half of Z0. 1/2 is the mistake of using only ZL in the denominator (50/100). With |Γ| = 1/3, VSWR = (1 + 1/3)/(1 − 1/3) = 2.0.

transmission-line-004.question: What is the VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio) when the magnitude of the reflection coefficient is |Γ| = 0.2?
transmission-line-004.explanation: VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|) = 1.2/0.8 = 1.5. On the line, the voltage is Vmax = V(1 + |Γ|) where the incident and reflected waves add, and Vmin = V(1 − |Γ|) where they cancel; the ratio of the two is the VSWR. 1.2 is only the numerator (1 + |Γ|), and 1.25 is 1/(1 − |Γ|), forgetting the numerator. To go the other way from VSWR, use |Γ| = (VSWR − 1)/(VSWR + 1); for 1.5 that gives 0.5/2.5 = 0.2.

transmission-line-005.question: What is the return loss when the magnitude of the reflection coefficient is |Γ| = 0.1?
transmission-line-005.explanation: Return loss is the ratio of reflected power to incident power in dB: RL = −20 log₁₀|Γ| = −20 log₁₀ 0.1 = 20 dB. |Γ| is a voltage ratio, so 20 log is used; in terms of power, 1% is reflected. 10 dB is the mistake of using 10 log on a voltage ratio. 0.04 dB is the mismatch loss −10 log₁₀(1 − |Γ|²) = −10 log₁₀ 0.99 ≈ 0.044 dB, a different quantity that expresses how much the power reaching the load is reduced by the reflection. A larger return loss means a better match.

transmission-line-006.question: On a lossless line terminated in a mismatched load, what is the spacing between a voltage maximum of the standing wave and the adjacent minimum (λ is the wavelength on the line)?
transmission-line-006.explanation: A standing wave arises from interference between the incident and reflected waves. Moving λ/4 along the line changes the round-trip path by λ/2, so the phase difference between the incident and reflected waves changes by 180°, and a voltage maximum turns into a minimum λ/4 away. λ/2 is the spacing between two maxima (or two minima), and λ is two periods of the standing-wave pattern. With a purely resistive load, the load end is a voltage maximum if ZL > Z0 and a minimum if ZL < Z0, and the impedance there is a pure resistance of Z0·VSWR or Z0/VSWR, respectively.

transmission-line-007.question: A 50 Ω line is terminated in a load ZL = 50 + j50 Ω. Which value is closest to the VSWR?
transmission-line-007.explanation: Γ = (ZL − Z0)/(ZL + Z0) = j50/(100 + j50), with magnitude |Γ| = 50/√(100² + 50²) = 50/111.8 ≈ 0.447. Then VSWR = (1 + 0.447)/(1 − 0.447) ≈ 2.62. Even though the resistive part equals 50 Ω, the reactive part causes a reflection, so the VSWR is not 1.0. About 1.4 is |ZL|/Z0 = 70.7/50, the mistake of applying VSWR = ZL/Z0, which holds only for purely resistive loads, to a complex load. This load can be matched by adding −j50 Ω (a capacitor) in series to cancel the reactance.

transmission-line-008.question: A 50 Ω line is to be matched to a 200 Ω load by inserting a single line that is λ/4 long at the design frequency (a quarter-wave transformer). What characteristic impedance should that line have?
transmission-line-008.explanation: A quarter-wave line transforms the load to Zin = Z1²/ZL, so making Zin = 50 Ω requires the geometric mean Z1 = √(Z0·ZL) = √(50 × 200) = √10000 = 100 Ω. As a check, 100²/200 = 50 Ω. 125 Ω is the arithmetic mean; using it gives 125²/200 ≈ 78 Ω, which does not match. 250 Ω is simply the sum. A quarter-wave transformer matches exactly only at the frequency where its length is exactly λ/4, so its bandwidth is limited; for a wider bandwidth, more sections are used.

transmission-line-009.question: When a lossless line with characteristic impedance Z0 is exactly a half wavelength (λ/2) long, what is the input impedance of the line terminated in a load ZL?
transmission-line-009.explanation: The input impedance of a lossless line is Zin = Z0 (ZL + jZ0 tan βl)/(Z0 + jZL tan βl), with β = 2π/λ. For l = λ/2, βl = π and tan π = 0, so Zin = Z0·ZL/Z0 = ZL: the load appears unchanged. Z0²/ZL is the value for l = λ/4 (βl = π/2, where tan goes to infinity), the principle of the quarter-wave transformer. The input is Z0 when the load is matched (ZL = Z0), regardless of length. Returning to the same value every λ/2 corresponds to one full turn on the Smith chart.

transmission-line-010.question: When a lossless line with a short-circuited end (a shorted stub) is shorter than λ/4, which correctly describes its input impedance?
choices: A capacitive reactance (it acts as a capacitor)
A pure resistance equal to Z0
An inductive reactance (it acts as an inductor)
transmission-line-010.explanation: For a short-circuit termination (ZL = 0), the input impedance is Zin = jZ0 tan βl. For 0 < βl < π/2 (lengths from 0 to λ/4), tan is positive, giving a positive reactance — the stub acts as an inductor. At λ/8, for example, tan(π/4) = 1 and Zin = +jZ0. The input is capacitive for a shorted stub between λ/4 and λ/2, or for an open stub shorter than λ/4 (Zin = −jZ0 cot βl). A lossless stub consumes no power, so it has no resistive part and never looks like a pure resistance equal to Z0.

transmission-line-011.question: A short-circuited stub that is λ/4 long at the design frequency, connected in shunt with the main line, has almost no effect on signals at that frequency. Which is the correct reason?
choices: The stub's input impedance is theoretically infinite (an open circuit)
The stub's input impedance is zero (a short circuit), so the signal passes straight through the stub
The stub's input impedance equals the Z0 of the main line
transmission-line-011.explanation: A quarter-wave line inverts impedance as Zin = Z0²/ZL, so the short at the far end (ZL = 0) looks like an open circuit (infinite impedance) at the input. Connecting an infinite impedance in shunt does nothing to the main line, so signals at the design frequency pass through unaffected. At DC, however, the stub is still a short, so it can be used to feed bias current or to provide a discharge path for static electricity. A quarter-wave open stub is the one whose input is zero; connected in shunt, it shorts out that frequency and blocks it. If the stub presented a resistance of Z0 in shunt, the main line would be mismatched.

transmission-line-012.question: For a coaxial cable with a velocity factor of 0.66, which physical length is closest to λ/4 for a 100 MHz signal? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
transmission-line-012.explanation: The free-space wavelength is λ0 = c/f = 3×10⁸/(100×10⁶) = 3 m, so λ/4 is 0.75 m. Inside the cable the wave travels at 0.66 times the speed of light, so the wavelength also shrinks by a factor of 0.66, and λ/4 becomes 0.75 × 0.66 ≈ 0.495 m, about 50 cm. About 75 cm is the free-space length that ignores the velocity factor, and about 114 cm is the mistake of dividing by the factor (0.75/0.66). The velocity factor is set by the relative permittivity εr of the dielectric as 1/√εr; for polyethylene (εr ≈ 2.25) it is about 0.66. Always include this shortening when cutting cables for stubs or phase matching.

transmission-line-013.question: The characteristic impedance of a coaxial line with inner-conductor outer diameter d and outer-conductor inner diameter D is Z0 = (60/√εr) ln(D/d) Ω. Which value is closest to Z0 when the line is filled with polyethylene of relative permittivity 2.25 and D/d = 3.5 (ln 3.5 ≈ 1.25)?
transmission-line-013.explanation: √εr = √2.25 = 1.5, so Z0 = (60/1.5) × 1.25 = 40 × 1.25 = 50 Ω. About 33 Ω comes from forgetting the square root and using 60/2.25, and about 75 Ω from ignoring the dielectric and calculating for air (εr = 1). For the same dimension ratio, filling the line with a dielectric increases the capacitance per unit length and lowers Z0. Also, Z0 grows only with the logarithm of D/d, so changing Z0 substantially requires a large change in the dimension ratio.

transmission-line-014.question: On a Smith chart there is a point whose impedance normalized to Z0 = 50 Ω is z = 1 + j1. What is the normalized admittance y at this point?
transmission-line-014.explanation: y = 1/z = 1/(1 + j1) = (1 − j1)/((1 + j1)(1 − j1)) = (1 − j1)/2 = 0.5 − j0.5. The actual impedance is 50 + j50 Ω, and the admittance is 0.01 − j0.01 S. An inductive impedance (+j) corresponds to a negative susceptance (−j), so the sign flips; 0.5 + j0.5 has the wrong sign. 1 − j1 is just the complex conjugate, without dividing by the squared magnitude. On the Smith chart, the y point is the z point rotated 180° about the center, the same position you reach by transforming through a λ/4 line.

transmission-line-015.question: On a lossless line, as line length is added from the load toward the generator (signal source), how does the point representing the input impedance move on the Smith chart?
choices: It moves clockwise on a circle centered on the center of the chart, making one full turn every λ/2
It moves counterclockwise on a circle centered on the center of the chart, making one full turn every λ/4
It moves along a constant-resistance circle, with only the reactance changing while the resistance stays at the load's value
transmission-line-015.explanation: On a lossless line the magnitude of the reflection coefficient does not change; only the phase varies with position, as Γ(l) = ΓL·e^(−j2βl). Moving toward the generator delays the phase, so the point travels clockwise on the circle around the center set by the VSWR (the constant-VSWR circle). 2βl reaches 2π when l = λ/2, so one full turn takes λ/2; at λ/4 the point has gone halfway around and z has moved to 1/z. Counterclockwise is the direction for moving back toward the load. Moving along a constant-resistance circle happens when a reactive element is added in series, not when the line is lengthened.
